t: Minimum Operations to Maximize Last Elements in Arrays
o: Swaps happen column-wise. We need nums1's last cell to hold the max of nums1 and nums2's last cell to hold the max of nums2. Only whether we swap the last column (0 or 1 operations) matters structurally; every other column is swapped at most once and only if forced. Example 3 is impossible because 5 sits above 5 and neither last cell can dominate both columns.
k: Enumerate just two cases: swap the last column or not — fixing the targets last1 = nums1[n-1], last2 = nums2[n-1].
Given targets, each earlier column is swapped iff needed, and a swap is possible iff nums1[i] ≤ last2 and nums2[i] ≤ last1; otherwise that case fails.

a.n: Approach 1: Enumerate Last-Column Swap + Greedy Check
a.i: For each case (swap last column or not), set the required maxima, then sweep columns 0..n-2: if a column already fits under both targets do nothing; else swap it if the swapped values fit; else the case is infeasible. Take the cheaper feasible case.
s: Define solve(swapped): optionally swap index n-1; let a = nums1[n-1], b = nums2[n-1].
For i < n-1: if nums1[i] > a or nums2[i] > b, require nums1[i] <= b and nums2[i] <= a, increment count; else fail.
Answer = min over both cases, or -1 if both fail.

w: The enumeration insight collapses an apparently exponential space into two cases because swapping a column twice is pointless and only the last column's identity matters. Pitfall: after swapping the last column, the targets themselves swap. Edge cases: n = 1 (answer 0 always), duplicate maxima. Follow-up: what if three arrays were involved?
